explanations.answer: What has been decreed must be accomplished
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives: “…for what has been decreed must be accomplished.” He will be successful until the time of wrath is completed, and not a day past it. He does as he pleases, but he's still working on a clock he didn't set. He thinks he's running the show, friend.

explanations.answer: The other kings are too afraid of him
explanations.explanation: The text never says the other kings are afraid of him. What it says is that he will be successful until the time of wrath is completed, “…for what has been decreed must be accomplished.” So his success has an end point that was set ahead of time. Fear didn't build it, and fear doesn't keep it going.

explanations.answer: His fathers left him a mighty kingdom
explanations.explanation: His fathers do come up in this passage, but only as the gods he will show no regard for (Daniel 11:37). Nothing is said about a kingdom they left him. The reason for his lasting is stated plainly: “…for what has been decreed must be accomplished.” That's the whole answer, no inheritance paperwork needed.

explanations.answer: A god of fortresses
explanations.explanation: That's the one. He honors “a god of fortresses—a god his fathers did not know—with gold, silver, precious stones, and riches.” Big walls, big treasure, big price tag. I've honored my oven plenty, friend, but never with precious stones.

explanations.answer: A god of the hills
explanations.explanation: Hills never come up here. The text says he honors “a god of fortresses,” and it's a god his fathers did not know. The gifts are gold, silver, precious stones and riches. Nobody's hauling jewels up a hill in this verse.

explanations.answer: A god of the valleys
explanations.explanation: No valleys in this verse, friend. The god he honors in place of the others is “a god of fortresses.” It's also a god his fathers did not know. The treasure he gives it is gold, silver, precious stones and riches.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, he will “…greatly honor those who acknowledge him, making them rulers over many and distributing the land for a price.” So there are rewards for the ones who side with him. It comes with a price tag, too, since the land is handed out for a price. I'd read that fine print twice, friend.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. He will “…greatly honor those who acknowledge him, making them rulers over many and distributing the land for a price.” So acknowledging him comes with honor and rulership. Not what you'd expect from a man with a fortress god, right?

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: One country would be a small trip, and this isn't one. The text says the king of the North will storm out with chariots, horsemen and many ships, “invading many countries and sweeping through them like a flood.” So it's many countries, not one. That's a lot of ships for one stop, friend.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right, it's many. The king of the North storms out with chariots, horsemen and many ships, “invading many countries and sweeping through them like a flood.” A flood doesn't stop at one backyard. That is a big, wide sweep.

explanations.answer: Edom and Moab and Ammon's leaders
explanations.explanation: Yes! The text says, “But these will be delivered from his hand: Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites.” Many countries fall when he invades the Beautiful Land, so those three being spared stands out. Notice it says the leaders of the Ammonites, not the whole country. Small detail, big difference.

explanations.answer: Tyre and Sidon and Philistia's lords
explanations.explanation: Those names don't appear in this verse. The text says that when he invades the Beautiful Land, many countries will fall, but “…these will be delivered from his hand: Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites.” Keep those three in your pocket, friend.

explanations.answer: Assyria and Elam and Babylon's princes
explanations.explanation: None of those show up here. The ones delivered from his hand are “Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites.” Many other countries fall around them. So the list is short, and it's a different list.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: The text says it plainly the other way: “…not even the land of Egypt will escape.” He extends his power over many countries, and Egypt is named right in that list. Then in the next verse he gains control of its treasures of gold and silver. Egypt does not get a free pass here.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right. “He will extend his power over many countries, and not even the land of Egypt will escape.” Egypt is named on purpose, so we know how far his reach goes. If Egypt can't slip away, nobody can.

explanations.answer: Go out in great fury to destroy many
explanations.explanation: That's exactly it. News from the east and the north alarms him, “and he will go out with great fury to destroy many and devote them to destruction.” He gets scared and then gets loud. Some folks answer a scary text with a nap. He answers it with an army.

explanations.answer: Send his riches back to make peace
explanations.explanation: The text has him doing nothing of the kind. News from the east and the north alarms him, and he “will go out with great fury to destroy many and devote them to destruction.” His riches stay in his hands. He chooses fury.

explanations.answer: Hide in the strongest fortress he has
explanations.explanation: That would be a quiet response, and this isn't quiet. The text says the news alarms him, “and he will go out with great fury to destroy many and devote them to destruction.” So he goes out, he doesn't hide. Fury wins over fortress here.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says. It says, “…he will meet his end with no one to help him.” Nobody rushes in. After all that conquering, he ends up completely on his own.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right. “…he will meet his end with no one to help him.” After all those countries, all those ships and all that gold, nobody steps in. I think that's a lonely spot to end up, friend.

explanations.answer: Everyone whose name is written in the book
explanations.explanation: Yes. Michael, the great prince who stands watch over Daniel's people, will rise up. And “…at that time your people—everyone whose name is found written in the book—will be delivered.” The key is the name in the book. Not a place, not a fight.

explanations.answer: Everyone who stays in the Beautiful Land
explanations.explanation: Where a person stays isn't the description given. Daniel is told that “…your people—everyone whose name is found written in the book—will be delivered.” It's about the name in the book. Location never makes the list.

explanations.answer: Everyone who stands and fights beside Michael
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anyone fights beside Michael, the great prince who stands watch over Daniel's people. It says he will rise up. Then it says that “…your people—everyone whose name is found written in the book—will be delivered.” So the answer is the name in the book.

explanations.answer: Shame and everlasting contempt
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, “some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.” It's a serious verse, and I won't joke about it. Two ways to wake up, and the text names both.

explanations.answer: A second life on the earth
explanations.explanation: A second earthly life isn't in the verse. The text says many who sleep in the dust will awake, “some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.” Those are the two outcomes it names. It's a heavy one, friend.

explanations.answer: Another sleep in the dust
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't send them back to sleep. It says many will awake, “some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.” So the others do wake up, and shame and contempt are what they wake to. It's a heavy verse, and the text gives exactly those two outcomes.

explanations.answer: Those who lead many to righteousness
explanations.explanation: Yes! “…those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.” Stars are close to my heart, since every finished cookie box lights up my sky with one. Forever and ever is a long time to shine, friend.

explanations.answer: Those who rule over many nations
explanations.explanation: Ruling over many nations isn't what earns it here. The text says “…those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.” It's about leading people toward righteousness, not about owning a map.

explanations.answer: Those who guard the holy mountain
explanations.explanation: The holy mountain comes up earlier, in verse 11:45, but not here. In this verse, “…those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.” Guarding isn't the job named. Leading many to righteousness is.

explanations.answer: Shut them up and seal the book
explanations.explanation: That's it. “But you, Daniel, shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end.” It's a book on hold, not a book thrown away. Sealed means it waits for a certain time.

explanations.answer: Read them aloud to the king
explanations.explanation: No king gets a reading in this verse. Daniel is told, “…shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end.” So the book stays closed for now. A sealed book makes for a quiet reading.

explanations.answer: Teach them to the people at once
explanations.explanation: The instruction goes the other direction. Daniel is told, “…shut up these words and seal the book until the time of the end.” That means nothing is handed out right away. The words wait.

explanations.answer: How long until these wonders are fulfilled
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the question. One of the two says to the man dressed in linen, “How long until the fulfillment of these wonders?” It's the kind of question we all want to ask. I've asked my oven the same thing, friend.

explanations.answer: Why the holy people must suffer so much
explanations.explanation: That question isn't asked here. One of the two says to the man dressed in linen, “How long until the fulfillment of these wonders?” It's a question about time. Nothing about why.

explanations.answer: Where the sealed book should be kept
explanations.explanation: Nobody asks where the book goes. What's asked of the man dressed in linen is, “How long until the fulfillment of these wonders?” Daniel was already told to seal the book. This question is about how long.

explanations.answer: A time and times and half a time
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. The man dressed in linen swears by Him who lives forever, “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time.” He raised both hands toward heaven to say it. It's the answer given, friend, even if it's not a date on a calendar.

explanations.answer: Seven weeks and sixty-two weeks
explanations.explanation: That's not what the man says. He raises both hands toward heaven, swears by Him who lives forever, and says, “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time.” That's the length he gives.

explanations.answer: Forty days and forty nights
explanations.explanation: That phrase turns up in other parts of the Bible, like the flood in Genesis 7:12. It isn't the answer here. The man dressed in linen swears by Him who lives forever, “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time.” That's the answer given in this vision.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Daniel says it himself: “I heard, but I did not understand.” Then he asks, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?” I've nodded along to a mixer manual like I knew what it said, so I get it. Daniel at least asks.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right. Daniel says, “I heard, but I did not understand.” So he asks, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?” Nothing shameful about it, friend. I once nodded at a recipe for ten minutes before admitting I had no idea what it meant.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, he's told, “None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand.” That comes right after he hears that many will be purified, made spotless and refined. So understanding goes with the wise. The wicked don't get it.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. Daniel is told, “None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand.” So the wise do understand. It's the wicked who don't.

explanations.answer: He will rest and then arise to his inheritance
explanations.explanation: That's the promise. “But as for you, go on your way until the end. You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.” After all those hard words, the last line is a gentle one. It's a good thing to hear at the end, friend.

explanations.answer: He will be taken up to heaven alive
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says, “You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.” Resting and then arising is what Daniel is promised. That's the promise on the page.

explanations.answer: He will rule over the Beautiful Land
explanations.explanation: Ruling over the Beautiful Land isn't promised to Daniel. He's told, “You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.” His inheritance is what's named. Nothing here says he'll rule anything.
